corpus_definition: Material that is used to make clothes or furniture covers.

forms.definition: cloth or material used for making clothes, curtains and covers
forms.example: This fabric feels very soft to the touch.
forms.note: Don't confuse with factory: fabric is cloth, not a building where things are made.

syn.note: Very close and very common: 'a dress made of soft material'.
Very close; cloth is a little more everyday.
More technical, used in industry and trade: 'the textile industry'.

forms.note: fabricate (to make, or to invent false information) shares an old Latin root but is not made from fabric.

context.text: My grandmother buys fabric at Chorsu Bazaar in Tashkent. She chooses a bright, soft fabric and makes new dresses for the whole family.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; fabricate listed as not_family (same Latin root, not derived from fabric).

corpus_definition: A fact or situation that influences a result.

forms.definition: one of the things that has an effect on a result or decision
forms.example: Price is a key factor in our choice.
forms.note: In maths it also means a number that divides another number exactly.

syn.note: Close: one part of a situation. A little more formal.
Related: a cause makes something happen; a factor is only one of the things that has an effect.
Related and easy: a reason explains why someone did something.
Related: an influence is the power to change something.
Related: one side or part of a situation, not always something that changes the result.

forms.definition: to include something as one thing to think about when you plan or decide
forms.example: We need to factor the cost of petrol into our travel plans.
forms.note: Usually 'factor in' or 'factor something into something'.

syn.note: Easy and general; factor in is about plans, costs and decisions.
Related: to think about something carefully before you decide.

ant.note: To leave something out of a plan or calculation.

forms.note: factorial exists only in maths and is very rare for learners.

context.text: Price was one factor, but the distance to school was another. When we chose a flat in Samarkand, we also factored in the noise from the busy road.

reviewer_note: factory looks related but is not a modern family member of factor; listed in people_not_family. Maths sense mentioned only in a note.

corpus_definition: to slowly lose colour, brightness, or strength

forms.note: There is no common noun; use the -ing form: 'the fading of the colours'.

forms.definition: to slowly become less bright, less strong or less clear
forms.example: The old photograph had faded to almost nothing.

syn.note: Related and easy: to go away completely. Fade is slower and may not be complete.
Close, but only for light: 'The lights dimmed.'
Related: to become less strong, for feelings, power or health.
Close, used for sounds and feelings: 'The music died away.'

ant.note: To become brighter or more colourful.

forms.definition: having lost its colour or brightness, often because it is old
forms.example: He always wears the same faded blue jeans.

syn.note: Close: light in colour, not strong.
Close: not bright or shiny.
Very close and informal: colours that look weak after much washing.

ant.note: Strong and full of light or colour.

forms.definition: slowly becoming weaker, less bright or less clear
forms.example: We walked home in the fading evening light.

context.text: My blue curtains slowly faded in the hot Tashkent sun. In the fading evening light they look even older, so my mother wants to buy new ones.

reviewer_note: No real noun in learner dictionaries (film 'fade-in/out' are compounds); both participle adjectives shown.

corpus_definition: To lose consciousness for a short time.

forms.definition: a short time when you lose consciousness and fall down
forms.example: She fell to the floor in a faint.
forms.note: Mostly in the phrase 'in a faint'.

syn.note: Close: a short time when you lose consciousness or memory.
Related: a sudden fall because you are ill or weak.

forms.definition: to suddenly lose consciousness for a short time and fall down
forms.example: An old man fainted in the heat at the bus stop.

syn.note: Very close and very common in everyday English.
Very close; also used when you can't remember what happened.
Related: to fall down suddenly; you may still be awake.
Old-fashioned or literary; often about strong feelings.

ant.note: To become conscious again after fainting.

forms.definition: feeling weak and as if you may lose consciousness
forms.example: She felt faint because of the extreme heat.
forms.note: Same spelling, another meaning: 'not strong or clear', as in 'a faint sound'.

syn.note: Close and easy: feeling that everything is turning around you.
Related and easy: without much strength.

forms.definition: in a way that is not strong or clear
forms.example: She smiled faintly and said nothing.
forms.note: Belongs to faint = not strong or clear (a faint sound), not losing consciousness.

context.text: On the hottest day of summer, an old man fainted at the bus stop in Bukhara. He told the doctor he had felt faint all morning.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: definition is the verb but the example uses the adjective (felt faint); map follows the verb definition and shows the adjective as a conversion.

corpus_definition: something or someone that you know well.

forms.definition: good knowledge of something because you have seen or used it often
forms.example: Her familiarity with the city helped us find the hotel quickly.

syn.note: Related: what you know; familiarity comes from seeing or using something often.
Formal: 'some acquaintance with the subject'.
Related and easy: knowledge you get by doing something.

ant.note: Not knowing about something at all.

forms.definition: to help yourself or someone learn about something new
forms.example: Take a few minutes to familiarize yourself with the new phone.
forms.note: British spelling: familiarise. Usually 'familiarize yourself with something'.

syn.note: Very close and formal: 'acquaint yourself with the rules'.
Related and easy: to get knowledge about something.

forms.definition: known to you because you have seen or heard it before
forms.example: That man looks familiar to me.

syn.note: Close and easy, but less natural before a noun.
Close: easy to know because you have seen it before. British: recognisable.
Related and easy: what happens or is seen most of the time.
Related: happening or seen often, but not always known to you.

ant.note: Easy: new and not known, sometimes a little worrying.
Not known by you or by most people.

forms.definition: in a friendly and informal way, as with friends
forms.example: He spoke familiarly to the teacher, which surprised everyone.
forms.note: Belongs to familiar = too friendly or informal, not 'known well'.

context.text: At first the streets of Tashkent were not familiar to me. I walked around every evening to familiarize myself with the city, and my familiarity with it grew fast.

reviewer_note: familiarly is a false friend (informal manner), shown as other_meaning. 'familiar with' has its own phrase map.

corpus_definition: to know something or someone quite well.
usage_note: be familiar with + noun / -ing: 'Are you familiar with this program?' Compare: 'This song is familiar to me' (the thing is familiar TO a person).

relations.note: Easy everyday verb: 'Do you know this program?'
Related: something is no longer new or strange for you: 'I'm used to the heat.'

context.text: Are you familiar with this computer program? My brother is, so he can help us. He became familiar with it at his job in Namangan.

reviewer_note: Phrase map; the person is the subject (familiar with), unlike 'familiar to'.

corpus_definition: To close or join two parts together tightly.

forms.note: The nouns fastener and fastening name things, so they are in People & things.

forms.definition: to close something or join two parts together so it stays closed
forms.example: Please fasten your seatbelt before the flight takes off.

syn.note: Very close and everyday, for buttons, coats and belts.
Close but more formal: to fix something so it cannot move.
Related: to join one thing to another.
Related and easy: to close or join with string or rope.
Related and easy, but more general.

ant.note: To open something that was closed with a button, belt or zip.

forms.definition: closed or joined so that it will not open
forms.example: Keep your seatbelt fastened while the car is moving.

syn.note: Close and easy, but more general.
Related: fixed and safe, so it cannot move.

forms.definition: firmly, so that it cannot move or come out
forms.example: The car was stuck fast in the deep mud.
forms.note: This is the old meaning that fasten comes from. Don't confuse with fast = quickly.

syn.note: Very close and common.
Close and easy.

people.definition: a small thing like a button, hook or zip that closes clothes or bags
people.example: The fastener on my bag is broken.

people.definition: a device such as a button, hook or zip used to close something
people.example: The dress has a fastening at the back.

context.text: Please fasten your seatbelt. The plane will not take off from Tashkent until every belt is fastened and every bag is in its place.

reviewer_note: fasten = fast (firmly) + -en; adverb fast shown in its 'firmly' meaning with a note on fast = quickly. Silent t noted.

corpus_definition: To want to have or do something at this moment.
usage_note: feel like + noun / -ing: 'I feel like pizza', 'I feel like going out.' Not followed by 'to do'. Often negative: 'I don't feel like cooking.'

relations.note: Easy and general; feel like is about a wish at this moment.
Very close, informal British English: 'Do you fancy a coffee?'
Related and polite: 'I would like a tea, please.'
Very close: 'I'm in the mood for a film.'

context.text: I feel like eating plov for dinner today. My sister doesn't feel like cooking, so we will go to the cafe near our house.

reviewer_note: Different from 'feel like' = seem/resemble ('It feels like rain'); map keeps only the 'want' meaning.

corpus_definition: A large boat that carries people or cars across a river or sea.

forms.definition: a boat that carries people and cars across water, usually on a regular trip
forms.example: We took the ferry across the river this morning.

syn.note: Related and easy: any vessel on water; a ferry is a boat with a regular route.
Related: a large boat, usually for the sea.

forms.definition: to carry people or things from one place to another, often again and again
forms.example: Small boats ferry tourists to the island every hour.
forms.note: Also used for cars and buses: 'Dad ferries the kids to school.'

syn.note: Close but more formal and general.
Close and easy.
Related and very easy: 'take the children to school'.

context.text: We took the ferry across the river this morning. In summer, a small boat ferries tourists to the island every hour.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows, same meaning: merged (B1). ferryman/ferryboat are compounds and left out.

corpus_definition: a thin thread-like part of a plant, fabric, or material

forms.definition: a very thin thread that plants, cloth and other materials are made of
forms.example: Cotton fibers are spun into thread at the factory.
forms.note: British spelling: fibre. In food, it also means the parts of plants that help digestion: 'Whole grains contain more fiber.'

syn.note: Close and easy; a thread is usually longer and made by people.
Close: one thin piece of hair, rope or thread.
Close but technical: a very thin thread, also the wire in a light bulb.

forms.definition: made of many thin threads, often tough to cut or chew
forms.example: The stems of this plant are tough and fibrous.

syn.note: Close and informal, often about food: 'stringy meat'.

context.text: Uzbek cotton is famous for its long, strong fibers. The stems of the cotton plant are fibrous, so farmers use them for fuel, not for food.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: example ('Whole grains contain more fiber') uses the food sense, not the thread sense in the definition; food sense mentioned in the note. No -ous affix claimed (fibr- is not a word).
